newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seen saving billions with open power market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen saving billions with open power market.

text.p: The U.S. government could save $88 billion to $246 billion over ten years if local power markets are opened to competition, a report released Thursday by a taxpayer group said.

Assuming that electricity prices would fall in a deregulated market, the report found the biggest savings would come on entitlement programs such as Social Security, Medicare and federal pension payments, while tax revenue would grow.

"The most important impact, by far, stems from the impact of falling electricity prices on the consumer price index (CPI), which is used to index many important entitlement programs and the personal income tax structure for inflation," the study by the Barents Group said.
The government would also save money on its own electricity bills and on the price of items it bought, as manufacturers' electricity costs fell, the report for the National Taxpayers Union said.

The analysis relied on models used in a study last year by the conservative Citizens for a Sound Economy group, which estimated that electricity prices would fall sharply in a competitive market. Critics of that study questioned its assumptions about how much electricity demand would change in an open market.
The Barents group found that if power prices fell 13 percent in the first year after deregulation and stayed at that level, the government would save $88 billion over 10 years.
If power prices fell 25 percent the first year and dropped 42 percent from today's levels over 10 years, then the government would save $217 billion over the period.
And in the most optimistic outlook, if power prices fell 25 percent the first year and dropped 42 percent over five years, the report said the government would save $246 billion over 10 years.

"Bringing consumer choice to electricity is one of the few ways to painlessly reduce the deficit while making consumers better off," David Keating, executive vice president of the National Taxpayers Union, said in a statement.
Lawmakers who are pushing to make states break up local utility monopolies said the report vindicated their efforts.

"Reasonable men and women can differ on the numbers. But there's one thing they won't argue with: that competition means savings, always, every time, without exception -- savings to households and savings to Uncle Sam," House Commerce Committee chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, said in a statement.
